newsitem.title: INDIA: India cyclone kills at least 510, thousands homeless.
newsitem.headline: India cyclone kills at least 510, thousands homeless.

text.p: A cyclone which swept the low-lying coastland of southeast India killed at least 510 people, possibly many more, destroying houses, livestock and crops, police and officials said on Friday.
Hyderabad police said the death toll was 510, while Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister Chandrababu Naidu said more than 1,000 may have been killed.
The cyclone struck late on Wednesday and raged for five hours before moving inland. State government spokesman Nageswara Rao put the number of homes destroyed or damaged at 400,000.

Around 3.5 million people live in the the fertile Konaseema region around the Godavari river delta south of the port of Kakinada which bore the full brunt of the storm. The area is the rice bowl of Andhra Pradesh.
Around two million people had been affected by the disaster, Rao said. He said the ministry had not assessed an exact death toll "because of the inaccessibility of places".
Most people were killed by flooding, house collapse or electrocutions caused by gale force winds and heavy rains which wrecked their rudimentary mud and thatch homes, officials said.
Around 40 people were killed when a ferry capsized in the Godavari river.
"The rice bowl of the state looks like a burial ground," the minister said after overflying the flooded areas by helicopter on Thursday.

H.S. Brahma, the official coordinating relief in Hyderabad, 200 miles (320 km) to the west of Kakinada, said more than 100,000 people were being sheltered in 178 relief camps set up in East and West Godavari districts.
The armed forces have been mobilised and Chief Minister Naidu has appealed to Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda to provide maxium assistance for the relief and rescue operation.

But communications and transport routes into the worst affected areas are severely disrupted and efforts to move help to the worst affected areas have been slowed by fallen trees, collapsed bridges, blocked roads and downed telephone lines.
Reddy Subramanium, a tax collector in Rajahmundry, East Godavari, said thousands of livestock had been lost, and 250,000 hectares (618,000 acres) of rice paddy inundated.
He said 450,000 hectares (1.1 million acres) of other crops, including chilies, banana plantations and coconut groves, had been damaged.
Subramaniam said several thousand cattle were killed. "We have a problem on our hands with the dead animals -- whether to burn them or bury them," he said.
Some areas of Kakinada were submerged after a tidal wave hit the town. "The water receded after an hour but stayed on in the low-lying areas," Subramaniam said.
There is a shortage of water in coastal villages in East Godavari because of the salt water flooding.
"Water is being transported from towns as far away as 200 km (125 miles)," Subramaniam said. "Food packets and kerosene are being distributed freely."
Port authorities had moved 12 ships anchored at Kakinada to a safety zone out to sea to escape the cyclone assault.
Naidu said he had asked naval and oil company helicopters to ferry doctors and medicine to help the injured, the Press Trust of India news agency said.
He also said the state electricity board had been told to restore power supply in the affected areas as soon as possible.
"Even if they work day and night, it will take a minimum of 15 days to restore power and water supply, he said.
